newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran awards Total SA huge gas contract.
newsitem.headline: Iran awards Total SA huge gas contract.

text.p: Iran's Foreign Affairs Minister Ali Akbar Velayati on Sunday said Iran had awarded French oil firm Total SA a $3.5 billion contract to lead the development of one of the world's single largest gas fields.

Total's contract to develop Iran's offshore South Pars field would represent the single largest investment in the Islamic republic since its 1979 revolution. It flies directly in the face of American trade sanctions imposed against Iran.

"Total has signed an agreement with the minister of oil of our country. The total amount of this contract is $3.5 billion. It belongs to South Pars which is an important field for gas," Velayati, through a translator, told a news conference in Tehran.
Velayati, talking about Iran's ability to defeat U.S. sanctions, said the South Pars contract was worth $3.5 billion.

Under Washington's Iran-Libya Sanctions Act signed by U.S. President Bill Clinton last year, the president has the power to impose sanctions on non-U.S. firms that invest $40 million or more a year in Iran's oil and gas sectors.
But the final status of the South Pars contract was unclear after Velayati's remarks.

An official at the National Iranian Oil Company (NIOC) in Tehran told Reuters that negotiations were still continuing with Total and also with a rival consortium led by the Anglo-Dutch Royal Dutch Shell Group.
"The foreign minister's statement is not correct as such. NIOC and the Ministry of Petroleum have not finalised any agreement with either Total or Shell," said a NIOC official.
"Our negotiations with the two sides are still continuing," the official added without elaborating.
Total and Shell have this month confirmed they have been in advanced negotiations with NIOC on South Pars but that a contract had not yet been signed.

The two firms are leading groups of European and Asian firms aiming to develop South Pars to produce two billion cubic feet a day of gas after five years of project work. That gas would be the main source of supply for Iran's plans to export gas to Turkey and Pakistan.
Iran has the world's second largest reserves of gas after Russia but exports dried up when it lost its main customer, the former Soviet Union, soon after 1979.

Velayati said the deal with Total, and the interest of European and American firms in an energy conference in the Iranian city of Isfahan earlier this month, showed that Washington's sanctions were having no impact on Iran.
"The managers of your oil companies are more clever than your people working in the (U.S) foreign ministry," he said in response to a question put by an American reporter.
"They know that if they don't take part...they will be behind European oil companies like Total, Elf, Agip and the others," Velayati said.
U.S. firms Mobil Corp, Amoco and Conoco were reported to have attended the Isfahan conference despite the backdrop of the Iran-Libya Sanctions Act.
The U.S. State Department is also investigating reports that NIOC has awarded a $140 million contract to a joint British-Canadian venture to develop its Balal oilfield.
